BOOKS.0.title: History of Islam
BOOKS.0.description: The history of Islamic civilisation from the Prophet Muhammad to today
BOOKS.0.chapters.0.title: The Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah)
BOOKS.0.chapters.0.content:
The Arabian Peninsula before Islam is called the "Age of Ignorance" (Jahiliyyah). Idol worship was widespread among the Arabs. There were more than 360 idols in the Kaaba; the greatest were Lat, Manat and Uzza.

Society was built on tribal structures, and wars between tribes were frequent. There were cruel customs such as burying baby girls alive. Slavery was common and women had no rights at all.

Yet the "Hanif" tradition left from Prophet Ibrahim had not completely disappeared. Some people refused to worship idols and believed in the One God. The Kaaba had been built by Ibrahim and Ismail and was still regarded as sacred.
BOOKS.0.chapters.1.title: The Birth of the Prophet Muhammad
BOOKS.0.chapters.1.content:
The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was born in Makkah in 571 CE, about 50–55 days after the "Event of the Elephant". In that event Abraha, the Abyssinian governor of Yemen, attacked the Kaaba with an army of elephants to destroy it and was destroyed by the flocks of birds (ababil) sent by Allah.

His father was Abdullah and his mother Amina. Abdullah died in Madinah on his way back from a trade journey before Muhammad was born, so Muhammad came into the world as an orphan.

Following the custom of the time, because the desert air was healthier, he was given to Halimah al-Sa'diyyah as a wet nurse and stayed with her for 4–5 years. During this period the "opening of the chest" (shaqq al-sadr) took place. His mother Amina died on the way back from Madinah when he was six, and he passed into the care of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib. When his grandfather also died when he was eight, his uncle Abu Talib took him in.
BOOKS.0.chapters.2.title: The First Revelation and Prophethood
BOOKS.0.chapters.2.content:
When Muhammad reached the age of 40, he began to retreat to the Cave of Hira near Makkah for reflection and worship. In Ramadan of 610, on Laylat al-Qadr, Jibril (peace be upon him) brought revelation for the first time.

The first five verses of Surah al-Alaq were revealed, beginning with the command "Read!": "Read in the name of your Lord who created – created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the most Generous – who taught by the pen – taught man that which he knew not."

Muhammad was deeply shaken by this event and returned home trembling. His wife Khadijah comforted him and took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a Christian who knew the Torah and the Gospel. He said it was the same angel (Namus) who had come to Moses, and that Muhammad's people would drive him out (Bukhari, Bad' al-Wahy 3).
BOOKS.0.chapters.3.title: The Meccan Period
BOOKS.0.chapters.3.content:
The Meccan period lasted about 13 years (610–622). The first three years were a period of secret preaching. Khadijah, Abu Bakr, Ali and Zayd ibn Harithah were among the first Muslims.

After the secret period, the open call began. Muhammad warned Quraysh from Mount Safa. The idolaters reacted, and Abu Lahab and Abu Jahl in particular began fierce opposition.

The Muslims were severely tortured. Bilal al-Habashi, Ammar ibn Yasir, Sumayyah (the first woman martyr), Yasir and many other companions were persecuted. As the pressure grew, some Muslims migrated to Abyssinia (615).

The idolaters imposed a harsh boycott that lasted three years (616–619). The Muslims and the Banu Hashim who protected them were besieged in Shi'b Abi Talib and lived in hunger and misery.

The year 619 was remembered as the "Year of Sorrow": Khadijah and Abu Talib died. Muhammad went to Ta'if but was stoned. After his return came the Mi'raj – the ascension to the heavens and the obligation of the five daily prayers.
BOOKS.0.chapters.4.title: The Hijra
BOOKS.0.chapters.4.content:
The migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622 is the most important turning point in Islamic history and is taken as the start of the Hijri calendar.

Through the pledges of Aqabah, the Muslims of Madinah invited Muhammad to their city. When the idolaters learned of this, they decided to kill him: one man was chosen from every tribe, and they planned to raid his house at night.

Ali protected him by lying in his bed. Muhammad and Abu Bakr slipped out secretly and took refuge in the Cave of Thawr. When the idolaters reached the entrance, they saw a spider's web and a dove's nest and did not look inside.

After three days in the cave they set out for Madinah. On reaching Quba they built the first mosque. They were welcomed into Madinah with great joy, and the hymn "Tala'a al-Badru 'Alayna" was sung on this occasion.
BOOKS.0.chapters.5.title: The Medinan Period
BOOKS.0.chapters.5.content:
The Medinan period lasted 10 years (622–632). Here the first core of the Islamic state was formed. The Prophet's Mosque was built, and brotherhood was declared between the Ansar (the Muslims of Madinah) and the Muhajirun (those who migrated from Makkah).

With the "Charter of Madinah", all groups in the city (Muslims, Jews and idolaters) were brought under one constitution. Some researchers count it among the earliest written constitutions.

Important battles:
• Battle of Badr (624): 313 Muslims won a miraculous victory over 1,000 idolaters.
• Battle of Uhud (625): hardship followed when the archers left their posts; 70 companions were martyred.
• Battle of the Trench (627): a trench was dug around the city against an enemy army of 10,000.

Treaties:
• Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628): though it seemed to go against the Muslims, it was described as "Fath al-Mubin" (a clear victory).
• Conquest of Makkah (630): Makkah was taken almost without bloodshed by an army of 10,000, and a general amnesty was declared.
BOOKS.0.chapters.6.title: The Era of the Four Caliphs
BOOKS.0.chapters.6.content:
After the Prophet's death, the era of the four great caliphs began (632–661). It is known as the "Khulafa al-Rashidun" (the Rightly Guided Caliphs).

Abu Bakr (632–634): the first caliph. He fought the Ridda wars against those who left the religion, began compiling the Qur'an into a single book, and started the conquests of Syria and Iraq.

Umar (634–644): the second caliph, famous for his justice. Jerusalem, Egypt, Persia and Syria were conquered. The diwan (state registry) was established and the Hijri calendar was introduced. He was martyred by a Zoroastrian slave.

Uthman (644–656): the third caliph. He had copies of the Qur'an made and sent to the provinces (the Uthmanic Mushaf). The Islamic navy was founded and Cyprus was conquered. He was martyred during the time of strife (fitna).

Ali (656–661): the fourth caliph. Internal conflicts such as the Battle of the Camel and the Battle of Siffin took place. He moved the seat of the caliphate to Kufa and was martyred by the Kharijites.
BOOKS.0.chapters.7.title: The Umayyads and the Abbasids
BOOKS.0.chapters.7.content:
The Umayyad State (661–750): after Ali's martyrdom, Mu'awiyah took the caliphate. Damascus became the capital, and the caliphate turned into a hereditary monarchy.

Under the Umayyads:
• Islam spread as far as Spain (al-Andalus)
• North Africa was fully conquered
• Muslims entered Turkestan
• Arabic became the official language
• Islamic architecture flourished (Dome of the Rock, Umayyad Mosque)

The Abbasid State (750–1258): the Umayyads were overthrown and the Abbasids came to power. Baghdad became the capital, and Islamic civilisation lived its "Golden Age".

Under the Abbasids:
• The Bayt al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom) was founded
• Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic
• Mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy advanced (al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, al-Farabi)
• Great cities and libraries were built
• In 1258 Baghdad fell to the Mongol invasion and the Abbasid caliphate came to an end
BOOKS.0.chapters.8.title: The Seljuks and the Ottomans
BOOKS.0.chapters.8.content:
The Turks' entry into Islam: the Turks accepted Islam en masse in the 10th century. The Karakhanids were the first Turkic state to accept Islam (in the 10th century, under Satuk Bughra Khan).

The Great Seljuk Empire (1037–1194):
• Tughril Beg entered Baghdad and freed the Abbasid caliph from the Shi'i Buyids
• Sultan Alp Arslan opened the gates of Anatolia to the Turks with the victory of Manzikert in 1071
• Under Malik-Shah the empire reached its widest borders
• The Nizamiyya madrasas were founded, among the first organised institutions of higher learning
• The Crusades were resisted

The Ottoman Empire (1299–1922):
• Founded by Osman Gazi in 1299
• In 1453 Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror conquered Istanbul
• In 1517 Selim I brought the caliphate to the Ottomans
• Under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached its peak
• It ruled across three continents for more than 600 years
• The sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the caliphate in 1924
BOOKS.0.chapters.9.title: The Modern Era
BOOKS.0.chapters.9.content:
Abolition of the caliphate (1924): with the founding of the Republic of Türkiye, the institution of the caliphate was abolished on 3 March 1924, leaving the Muslim world without a central authority.

The colonial era: in the 19th and 20th centuries most of the Muslim world came under British, French, Dutch and Italian colonial rule. India, Egypt, Algeria, Indonesia, Libya and many other countries lost their independence.

Independence movements: from the 1940s Muslim countries began to regain independence:
• Pakistan (1947)
• Indonesia (1949)
• Libya (1951)
• Algeria (1962)
• The Gulf states (1970s)

Today: about 2 billion Muslims live in the world, and 57 countries are members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Muslims live all over the world, and Islam continues to be the fastest-growing religion.

In the modern era, Islamic revival movements, Islamic finance, the halal industry and Islamic educational institutions have grown considerably.
BOOKS.1.title: Stories of the Prophets
BOOKS.1.description: The lives of the 25 prophets named in the Qur'an
BOOKS.1.chapters.0.title: Adam (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.0.content: The first human and the first prophet. His descent from Paradise to earth, his repentance, and the story of his sons Habil and Qabil.
BOOKS.1.chapters.1.title: Idris (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.1.content: A prophet of knowledge and wisdom who was raised to a high station. He is known as the first person to write.
BOOKS.1.chapters.2.title: Nuh (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.2.content: He called his people to Allah for 950 years. The story of the great flood and the ark. One of the Ulul-Azm prophets.
BOOKS.1.chapters.3.title: Hud (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.3.content: Sent to the people of 'Ad. His people were destroyed by a violent wind.
BOOKS.1.chapters.4.title: Salih (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.4.content: Sent to the people of Thamud. As a miracle, a she-camel came forth from the rock. His people were destroyed by a terrible blast.
BOOKS.1.chapters.5.title: Ibrahim (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.5.content: Khalilullah (the friend of Allah). Being thrown into the fire, the sacrifice of his son Ismail, and the building of the Kaaba. One of the Ulul-Azm prophets.
BOOKS.1.chapters.6.title: Lut (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.6.content: The nephew of Ibrahim. Sent to the people of Sodom and Gomorrah. His people were destroyed.
BOOKS.1.chapters.7.title: Ismail (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.7.content: The son of Ibrahim. The story of the sacrifice. He helped build the Kaaba. Ancestor of the Arabs.
BOOKS.1.chapters.8.title: Ishaq (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.8.content: The son of Ibrahim. Ancestor of the Children of Israel. Born to his mother in her old age.
BOOKS.1.chapters.9.title: Ya'qub (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.9.content: The son of Ishaq. He had 12 sons. The story of Yusuf. He is also called Israel.
BOOKS.1.chapters.10.title: Yusuf (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.10.content: The most beautiful story. Thrown into a well by his brothers, he became a slave in Egypt, was imprisoned, and then became Egypt's minister of the treasury.
BOOKS.1.chapters.11.title: Ayyub (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.11.content: The prophet of patience. He remained patient despite severe illness, and Allah restored his health.
BOOKS.1.chapters.12.title: Shu'ayb (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.12.content: Sent to the people of Madyan. He commanded them not to cheat in measure and weight.
BOOKS.1.chapters.13.title: Musa (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.13.content: Kalimullah (the one to whom Allah spoke). His struggle against Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, and revelation on Mount Sinai. One of the Ulul-Azm prophets.
BOOKS.1.chapters.14.title: Harun (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.14.content: The brother and helper of Musa. Known for his eloquent speech.
BOOKS.1.chapters.15.title: Dawud (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.15.content: Both prophet and king. He was given the Zabur (Psalms). The miracle of softening iron. He had a beautiful voice.
BOOKS.1.chapters.16.title: Sulayman (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.16.content: The son of Dawud. He understood the speech of birds and ants, and the jinn and the wind were placed under his command. The story of Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba.
BOOKS.1.chapters.17.title: Ilyas (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.17.content: Sent to the Children of Israel. He warned his people who worshipped the idol Baal.
BOOKS.1.chapters.18.title: Al-Yasa' (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.18.content: The prophet who came after Ilyas. Among the virtuous.
BOOKS.1.chapters.19.title: Yunus (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.19.content: Swallowed by a whale, he prayed in the darkness and his repentance was accepted. Sent to the people of Nineveh.
BOOKS.1.chapters.20.title: Zakariyya (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.20.content: The guardian of Maryam. In his old age he asked for Yahya, and his prayer was answered.
BOOKS.1.chapters.21.title: Yahya (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.21.content: The son of Zakariyya and cousin of 'Isa. A prophet who was martyred.
BOOKS.1.chapters.22.title: 'Isa (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.22.content: Born without a father, he spoke in the cradle. The miracle of raising the dead. He was given the Injil (Gospel) and was raised to the heavens. One of the Ulul-Azm prophets.
BOOKS.1.chapters.23.title: Dhul-Kifl (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.23.content: A patient and virtuous prophet. He was given a name meaning "double portion".
BOOKS.1.chapters.24.title: Muhammad (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.1.chapters.24.content: The final prophet and the master of the prophets. The Qur'an was revealed to him. His community is the largest. One of the Ulul-Azm prophets.
BOOKS.2.title: The Life of the Prophet (Seerah)
BOOKS.2.description: The detailed life story of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)
BOOKS.2.chapters.0.title: Birth and childhood
BOOKS.2.chapters.0.content: Born in Makkah in 571, after the Event of the Elephant. Given to Halimah as a wet nurse. The opening of the chest. His mother's death and his grandfather's care.
BOOKS.2.chapters.1.title: Youth
BOOKS.2.chapters.1.content: He worked in trade and received the title "Muhammad al-Amin" (Muhammad the Trustworthy). He took part in the Fijar war and joined the Hilf al-Fudul alliance.
BOOKS.2.chapters.2.title: Marriage to Khadijah
BOOKS.2.chapters.2.content: At 25 he married Khadijah, and they shared 25 years of happy marriage. They had six children: Qasim, Abdullah, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah.
BOOKS.2.chapters.3.title: The first revelation
BOOKS.2.chapters.3.content: While worshipping in the Cave of Hira, the first revelation came in 610. Khadijah's comfort and Waraqah ibn Nawfal's confirmation.
BOOKS.2.chapters.4.title: The secret call
BOOKS.2.chapters.4.content: Three years of secret preaching. The first Muslims: Khadijah, Abu Bakr, Ali and Zayd ibn Harithah.
BOOKS.2.chapters.5.title: The open call
BOOKS.2.chapters.5.content: The open call from Mount Safa. The hostility of Quraysh began, along with torture and the migration to Abyssinia.
BOOKS.2.chapters.6.title: The boycott years
BOOKS.2.chapters.6.content: For three years they lived under siege in the quarter of Abu Talib and went through very hard days.
BOOKS.2.chapters.7.title: The Year of Sorrow
BOOKS.2.chapters.7.content: The deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib. The journey to Ta'if and the insults he faced there.
BOOKS.2.chapters.8.title: Isra and Mi'raj
BOOKS.2.chapters.8.content: In one night, from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa and from there the ascension to the heavens. The five daily prayers were made obligatory.
BOOKS.2.chapters.9.title: The pledges of Aqabah
BOOKS.2.chapters.9.content: Meetings with the Muslims of Madinah and the planning of the Hijra.
BOOKS.2.chapters.10.title: The Hijra
BOOKS.2.chapters.10.content: The migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622. Three days in the Cave of Thawr. Building the Quba Mosque.
BOOKS.2.chapters.11.title: The first years in Madinah
BOOKS.2.chapters.11.content: Brotherhood between the Ansar and the Muhajirun. Building the Prophet's Mosque. The Charter of Madinah.
BOOKS.2.chapters.12.title: The Battle of Badr
BOOKS.2.chapters.12.content: In 624, 313 Muslims won a victory over 1,000 idolaters – the first great victory.
BOOKS.2.chapters.13.title: The Battle of Uhud
BOOKS.2.chapters.13.content: The battle of 625. The hardship that followed when the archers left their posts.
BOOKS.2.chapters.14.title: The Battle of the Trench
BOOKS.2.chapters.14.content: In 627 a trench was dug against the enemy besieging Madinah – a psychological victory.
BOOKS.2.chapters.15.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
BOOKS.2.chapters.15.content: The treaty of 628. Seemingly unfavourable, it ended in a great victory.
BOOKS.2.chapters.16.title: The conquest of Makkah
BOOKS.2.chapters.16.content: In 630 Makkah was conquered almost without bloodshed by an army of 10,000, and a general amnesty was declared.
BOOKS.2.chapters.17.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage
BOOKS.2.chapters.17.content: The last Hajj, in 632. The Farewell Sermon and the verse "This day I have perfected for you your religion".
BOOKS.2.chapters.18.title: His passing
BOOKS.2.chapters.18.content: He passed away in Madinah in 632 at the age of 63 and was buried in the Rawdah.
BOOKS.3.title: Lives of the Companions
BOOKS.3.description: Exemplary lives of the Prophet's companions
BOOKS.3.chapters.0.title: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.0.content:
Known by the title "al-Siddiq" (the truthful), Abu Bakr was the Prophet's closest friend and the first caliph of Islam. Even before Islam he was a respected merchant.

He was the first free man to believe. He received the title "al-Siddiq" because he accepted the Mi'raj without hesitation. He accompanied the Prophet on the Hijra, and they hid together in the Cave of Thawr.

He spent all his wealth for Islam and bought and freed persecuted slaves such as Bilal al-Habashi. After the Prophet's death he was chosen as caliph (632–634). He fought the Ridda wars against those who left the religion and began compiling the Qur'an into a single book. He died in 634 and was buried beside the Prophet.
BOOKS.3.chapters.1.title: Umar (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.1.content:
Known by the title "al-Faruq" (the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood), Umar was the second caliph of Islam. Before becoming Muslim he was one of the fiercest enemies of Islam.

When he learned from Nu'aym ibn Abdullah that his own sister had become Muslim, he went to her house. Hearing Surah Ta-Ha there, his heart softened and he became Muslim. With his conversion the Muslims gained strength and began to pray openly.

During his caliphate (634–644) Jerusalem, Egypt, Persia and Syria were conquered. He is famous for his justice and would go among the people at night in disguise to hear their problems. He set up the diwan, started a salary system and introduced the Hijri calendar. In 644 he was stabbed by a Zoroastrian slave while praying and was martyred.
BOOKS.3.chapters.2.title: Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.2.content:
Known as "Dhun-Nurayn" (possessor of the two lights), Uthman received this name because he married two of the Prophet's daughters (Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum). He was the third caliph of Islam.

He was one of the first Muslims and a very wealthy merchant, known for his generosity. On the Tabuk expedition he alone equipped a third of the army. He bought the well of Rumah and endowed it to the Muslims.

During his caliphate (644–656) he had copies of the Qur'an made and sent to every province (the Uthmanic Mushaf). The first major naval battle in Islamic history (Dhat al-Sawari, 655) took place, and Cyprus was conquered. During the strife he was martyred while reading the Qur'an by rebels who had besieged his house (656).
BOOKS.3.chapters.3.title: Ali (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.3.content:
Known as "Asadullah" (the Lion of Allah) and "Haydar-i Karrar", Ali was the son of the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib and the Prophet's son-in-law. He was the fourth caliph of Islam.

He was the first child to become Muslim (at the age of 10). On the night of the Hijra he protected the Prophet by lying in his bed. He married Fatimah and was the father of Hasan and Husayn. He was known for his courage and heroism; at Khaybar he tore off the fortress gate and used it as a shield.

His knowledge was very deep. The narration "I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate" is well known, although hadith scholars have disputed its authenticity. During his caliphate (656–661) internal conflicts such as the Battle of the Camel and the Battle of Siffin took place. He moved the seat of the caliphate to Kufa and was martyred by the Kharijites in 661 on his way to prayer.
BOOKS.3.chapters.4.title: Talhah (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.4.content:
One of the ten companions promised Paradise (al-Ashara al-Mubashshara). He is remembered as "Talhat al-Khayr" (Talhah the good) and "Talhat al-Jud" (Talhah the generous).

At the Battle of Uhud he risked his life to protect the Prophet and received more than 70 wounds. He caught arrows with his hand, which was left disabled. The Prophet said: "Talhah has earned Paradise."

He was a very rich and generous companion, known for giving his wealth to those in need. He was martyred at the Battle of the Camel (656).
BOOKS.3.chapters.5.title: Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.5.content:
One of the ten promised Paradise. He is called "Hawari al-Rasul" (the disciple of the Messenger). He was Khadijah's nephew and the son of Safiyyah, the Prophet's paternal aunt.

He was the first companion to draw a sword for Islam. He became Muslim at 16 and took part in every battle, including Badr, Uhud and the Trench, becoming famous for his courage.

He played an important role in the conquest of Egypt and served as an adviser to Abu Bakr and Umar. He was martyred at the Battle of the Camel (656).
BOOKS.3.chapters.6.title: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.6.content:
One of the ten promised Paradise. Before Islam his name was Abd Amr; the Prophet changed it to Abd al-Rahman.

He was among the first Muslims, becoming Muslim through Abu Bakr. He took part in the migrations to Abyssinia and Madinah. He was a very successful merchant but spent most of his earnings in the way of Islam.

He gave generously for the Tabuk expedition. After Umar's martyrdom he served on the committee that chose the caliph. He never held back from good works and constantly helped the poor. He died in Madinah in 652.
BOOKS.3.chapters.7.title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.7.content:
One of the ten promised Paradise and the first companion to shoot an arrow for Islam. He is called the Prophet's maternal uncle because he belonged to Banu Zuhrah, the clan of the Prophet's mother Aminah.

He became Muslim at 17 and was among the first Muslims. At Uhud he shot arrows to protect the Prophet, who said: "Shoot, O Sa'd! May my father and mother be ransomed for you!" Ali said he never heard the Prophet say this to anyone but Sa'd (Bukhari).

Under Umar he commanded at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah (636) and conquered much of Persia. He founded the city of Kufa and stayed away from the strife. He died near Madinah in 675.
BOOKS.3.chapters.8.title: Sa'id ibn Zayd (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.8.content:
One of the ten promised Paradise. He was the husband of Fatimah, Umar's sister. His father Zayd ibn Amr was a Hanif who did not worship idols even before Islam.

The verses (Surah Ta-Ha) that led Umar to Islam were being recited in his house. He was among the first Muslims and took part in every battle except Badr (where he was on a special mission).

He played an important role in the conquest of Damascus. He was a humble and God-fearing man and died in Madinah in 671.
BOOKS.3.chapters.9.title: Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.9.content:
One of the ten promised Paradise. The Prophet described him as "Amin al-Ummah" (the trustworthy one of the community).

He was among the first Muslims. At the Battle of Badr he came face to face with his father and was forced to kill him. It grieved him deeply, but he had sacrificed everything for Islam.

Under Abu Bakr he was one of the commanders sent to Syria; Umar made him commander-in-chief of the armies there. Under Umar he carried out the conquest of Damascus, Jerusalem and Palestine. He was martyred in the plague of Amwas (Palestine) in 639.
BOOKS.3.chapters.10.title: Bilal al-Habashi (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.10.content:
The first muezzin of Islam. He was a slave of Abyssinian origin. When his cruel master Umayyah ibn Khalaf learned that he had become Muslim, he tortured him severely.

He was laid on burning sand under the scorching sun with huge rocks placed on his chest. When told "Worship the idols!", he only said "Ahad! Ahad!" (Allah is One!). Abu Bakr bought him and set him free.

At the conquest of Makkah he climbed onto the Kaaba and called the adhan. After the Prophet's death he was overcome with grief and no longer called the adhan (except once, at Umar's insistence). He went to Damascus and died there in 640.
BOOKS.3.chapters.11.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.11.content:
The great commander known as "Sayfullah" (the Sword of Allah), a title given to him by the Prophet. He is reported never to have been defeated in battle.

At the Battle of Uhud (while still an idolater) he attacked through the pass left by the archers and inflicted heavy losses on the Muslims. He became Muslim in 629. At the Battle of Mu'tah, after three commanders were martyred, he took command and saved the army.

Under Abu Bakr he won great successes in the Ridda wars. At the Battle of Yarmuk (636) he defeated the large Byzantine army. When Umar removed him from command he did not object and continued to fight as an ordinary soldier. He died in Homs in 642.
BOOKS.3.chapters.12.title: Mus'ab ibn Umayr (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.12.content:
He was the son of one of the wealthiest families in Makkah. In his youth he lived in luxury, wore the most expensive clothes and the finest perfumes.

When he became Muslim his family drove him out and deprived him of all his wealth. He suffered hunger and poverty but did not give up his faith. After the first pledge of Aqabah he was sent to Madinah to teach Islam – the first envoy of Islam.

At the Battle of Uhud he was the standard-bearer. When his right hand was cut off he took the banner in his left; when that too was cut off he held it with his arms. He did not let go of the banner until his last breath and was martyred. His shroud was too short: when his head was covered his feet showed, so his feet were covered with idhkhir grass (Bukhari).
BOOKS.3.chapters.13.title: Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.13.content:
A Persian companion. Originally a Zoroastrian, he later became a Christian. When monks told him "The final prophet will arise in the land of the Arabs", he set out on the journey.

On the way he was sold as a slave. When he came to Madinah he found the Prophet and became Muslim, and the Prophet helped him gain his freedom. He was honoured with the hadith "Salman is one of us, the People of the House."

At the Battle of the Trench (627) he suggested digging a trench around the city – a Persian war tactic unknown to the Arabs. Under Umar he served as governor of al-Mada'in. He lived very humbly and died in 656.
BOOKS.3.chapters.14.title: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)
BOOKS.3.chapters.14.content:
The companion who narrated the most hadiths – 5,374 in total. His real name was Abd al-Rahman. Because he had a little cat, he became known as "Abu Hurayrah" (father of the kitten).

He became Muslim after the Battle of Khaybar (628) and never left the Prophet's side. He was one of the People of the Suffah – the poor companions who lived in the Prophet's Mosque to seek knowledge.

His memory was very strong. One day he said to the Prophet, "I forget what I hear from you." The Prophet told him to spread out his cloak and prayed for him, and from that day he forgot nothing. He served as mufti and judge in Madinah and died there in 678.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.title: Forty Hadith
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.description: Selections from Imam al-Nawawi's Forty Hadith and other sahih sources
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.0.explanation: Intention matters greatly in every deed. Allah looks at the intention in the heart rather than the outward form of what is done.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.1.explanation: Islam is built on testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establishing prayer, giving zakat, performing Hajj and fasting Ramadan.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.2.explanation: Faith has seventy-some levels. The highest is saying "La ilaha illallah" and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is also a branch of faith.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.3.text: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.3.explanation: A true believer wants for his brother in faith the good things he wants for himself. Selfishness stands in the way of perfect faith.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.4.text: The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.4.explanation: Both the lawful and the unlawful have been made clear, but between them are doubtful matters. Whoever avoids doubtful matters protects his religion and his honour.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.5.text: In the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.5.explanation: Truly, in the body there is a piece of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.6.explanation: The religion is sincerity: towards Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and all Muslims.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.7.text: A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.7.explanation: The blood, property and honour of every Muslim are sacred to every other Muslim. A Muslim does not wrong a Muslim, abandon him or look down on him.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.8.text: Avoid what I have forbidden you.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.8.explanation: When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you something, do as much of it as you are able.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.9.text: Allah is pure and accepts only what is pure.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.0.items.9.explanation: Allah is Tayyib (pure) and accepts only what is pure. Lawful earnings and a pure intention are conditions for acts of worship to be accepted.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.title: The Pillars of Islam
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.0.title: The Shahada
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.0.text: Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.0.explanation: Testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.1.title: Prayer
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.1.explanation: The Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha prayers are an individual obligation (fard 'ayn).
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.2.title: Fasting
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.2.text: Fasting in the month of Ramadan
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.2.explanation: Abstaining from eating, drinking and marital relations from the start of Fajr until sunset.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.3.title: Zakat
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.3.explanation: Giving one-fortieth of wealth that has reached the nisab to those in need.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.4.title: Hajj
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.4.text: Performing Hajj for those who are able
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.1.items.4.explanation: Visiting the Kaaba once in a lifetime for those who are financially and physically able.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.title: The Articles of Faith
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.0.title: Belief in Allah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.0.text: Believing in the existence and oneness of Allah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.0.explanation: Allah is One and has no partner. He is the Creator of everything.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.1.title: Belief in the angels
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.1.text: Believing in the existence of the angels
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.1.explanation: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, Azra'il and the other angels.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.2.title: Belief in the books
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.2.explanation: The Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Qur'an.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.3.title: Belief in the prophets
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.3.explanation: All the prophets from Adam to Muhammad.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.4.title: Belief in the Last Day
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.4.text: Believing in the Day of Judgement and the Hereafter
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.4.explanation: Death, the grave, the Resurrection, the reckoning, Paradise and Hell.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.5.title: Belief in divine decree
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.5.text: Believing in divine decree, that good and evil come from Allah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.2.items.5.explanation: Everything is within Allah's knowledge and decree.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.title: Glossary of Religious Terms
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.0.name: Aqidah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.0.meaning: The field of knowledge dealing with the articles of faith
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.0.explanation: It studies the matters of belief in Islam.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.1.name: Bid'ah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.1.explanation: Religious practices that did not exist in the time of the Prophet.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.2.name: Fard
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.2.meaning: Obligatory worship established by definitive evidence
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.2.explanation: Acts of worship that bring reward when done and sin when abandoned.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.3.name: Wajib
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.3.meaning: An obligation one degree below fard
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.3.explanation: Such as the witr prayer and offering a sacrifice (in the Hanafi school).
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.4.name: Sunnah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.4.meaning: The sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.4.explanation: Divided into emphasised sunnah (mu'akkadah) and non-emphasised sunnah (ghayr mu'akkadah).
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.5.name: Mubah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.5.meaning: What one is free to do or leave
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.5.explanation: Such as lawful foods or drinking sherbet.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.6.name: Makruh
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.6.explanation: Divided into makruh tahrimi and makruh tanzihi.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.7.name: Haram
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.7.explanation: Major sins such as alcohol, gambling, usury and adultery.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.8.name: Hadith
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.8.explanation: Classified into grades such as sahih, hasan and da'if.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.9.name: Tafsir
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.9.meaning: Explanation of the verses of the Qur'an
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.9.explanation: Divided into tafsir by narration (riwayah) and tafsir by reasoning (dirayah).
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.10.name: Ijtihad
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.10.explanation: Legal interpretation carried out by qualified scholars (mujtahids).
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.11.name: Taqwa
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.11.meaning: Being mindful of Allah and avoiding sins
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.11.explanation: Keeping away from the forbidden and turning to the lawful.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.12.name: Tawakkul
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.12.meaning: Trusting in Allah and relying on Him
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.12.explanation: Taking the means and leaving the outcome to Allah.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.13.name: Ihsan
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.13.meaning: Worshipping Allah as if you see Him
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.13.explanation: Even if you do not see Allah, He sees you.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.14.name: Shirk
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.4.items.14.explanation: The greatest sin; it is not forgiven if one dies upon it without repenting.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.title: Prayer surahs
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.description: Short surahs recited in the prayer
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.0.title: Surah Al-Fatihah
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.0.text: Bismillahir-rahmanir-rahim. Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin. Ar-rahmanir-rahim. Maliki yawmid-din. Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Ihdinas-siratal-mustaqim. Siratal-ladhina an'amta 'alayhim ghayril-maghdubi 'alayhim wa lad-dallin.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.0.explanation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. [All] praise is [due] to Allah, Lord of the worlds - The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful, Sovereign of the Day of Recompense. It is You we worship and You we ask for help. Guide us to the straight path - The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked [Your] anger or of those who are astray.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.1.title: Surah Al-Ikhlas
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.1.text: Qul huwallahu ahad. Allahus-samad. Lam yalid wa lam yulad. Wa lam yakun lahu kufuwan ahad.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.1.explanation: Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One, Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, Nor is there to Him any equivalent."
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.2.title: Surah Al-Falaq
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.2.text: Qul a'udhu bi-rabbil-falaq. Min sharri ma khalaq. Wa min sharri ghasiqin idha waqab. Wa min sharrin-naffathati fil-'uqad. Wa min sharri hasidin idha hasad.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.2.explanation: Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak From the evil of that which He created And from the evil of darkness when it settles And from the evil of the blowers in knots And from the evil of an envier when he envies."
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.3.title: Surah An-Nas
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.3.text: Qul a'udhu bi-rabbin-nas. Malikin-nas. Ilahin-nas. Min sharril-waswasil-khannas. Alladhi yuwaswisu fi sudurin-nas. Minal-jinnati wan-nas.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.3.explanation: Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, The Sovereign of mankind. The God of mankind, From the evil of the retreating whisperer - Who whispers [evil] into the breasts of mankind - From among the jinn and mankind."
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.4.title: Surah Al-Kawthar
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.4.text: Inna a'taynakal-kawthar. Fa-salli li-rabbika wanhar. Inna shani'aka huwal-abtar.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.4.explanation: Indeed, We have granted you, [O Muhammad], al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice [to Him alone]. Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.5.title: Surah Al-'Asr
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.5.text: Wal-'asr. Innal-insana lafi khusr. Illal-ladhina amanu wa 'amilus-salihati wa tawasaw bil-haqqi wa tawasaw bis-sabr.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.5.explanation: By time, Indeed, mankind is in loss, Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.6.title: Surah Al-Fil
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.6.text: Alam tara kayfa fa'ala rabbuka bi-ashabil-fil. Alam yaj'al kaydahum fi tadlil. Wa arsala 'alayhim tayran ababil. Tarmihim bi-hijaratin min sijjil. Fa-ja'alahum ka-'asfin ma'kul.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.6.explanation: Have you not considered, [O Muhammad], how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, Striking them with stones of hard clay, And He made them like eaten straw.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.7.title: Surah Quraysh
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.7.text: Li-ilafi Quraysh. Ilafihim rihlatash-shita'i was-sayf. Fal-ya'budu rabba hadhal-bayt. Alladhi at'amahum min ju'in wa amanahum min khawf.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.7.explanation: For the accustomed security of the Quraysh - Their accustomed security [in] the caravan of winter and summer - Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them, [saving them] from hunger and made them safe, [saving them] from fear.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.8.title: Surah Al-Ma'un
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.8.text: Ara'aytal-ladhi yukadhdhibu bid-din. Fa-dhalikal-ladhi yadu''ul-yatim. Wa la yahuddu 'ala ta'amil-miskin. Fa-waylul lil-musallin. Alladhina hum 'an salatihim sahun. Alladhina hum yura'un. Wa yamna'unal-ma'un.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.8.explanation: Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? For that is the one who drives away the orphan And does not encourage the feeding of the poor. So woe to those who pray [But] who are heedless of their prayer - Those who make show [of their deeds] And withhold [simple] assistance.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.9.title: Surah Al-Kafirun
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.9.text: Qul ya ayyuhal-kafirun. La a'budu ma ta'budun. Wa la antum 'abiduna ma a'bud. Wa la ana 'abidum-ma 'abadtum. Wa la antum 'abiduna ma a'bud. Lakum dinukum wa liya din.
RELIGIOUS_TEXTS.3.items.9.explanation: Say, "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship. Nor are you worshippers of what I worship. Nor will I be a worshipper of what you worship. Nor will you be worshippers of what I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is my religion."
EDUCATION.0.title: Basic Islamic Knowledge
EDUCATION.0.description: Core topics every Muslim should know
EDUCATION.0.topics.0.title: Ablution (wudu)
EDUCATION.0.topics.0.content: The purification required for prayer. Its obligatory parts (Hanafi): washing the face, washing the arms including the elbows, wiping a quarter of the head, and washing the feet including the ankles.
EDUCATION.0.topics.1.title: Full ritual bath (ghusl)
EDUCATION.0.topics.1.content: Purification from major ritual impurity. Its obligatory parts (Hanafi): rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose and washing the whole body.
EDUCATION.0.topics.2.title: Dry ablution (tayammum)
EDUCATION.0.topics.2.content: Purification with earth when water is not available or cannot be used.
EDUCATION.0.topics.3.title: Prayer times
EDUCATION.0.topics.3.content: Determining the times of Fajr, sunrise, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha.
EDUCATION.0.topics.4.title: The obligatory elements of prayer
EDUCATION.0.topics.4.content: Conditions: purity from ritual impurity, purity from physical impurity, covering the awrah, facing the qibla, the prayer time and the intention. Pillars: the opening takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration and the final sitting.
EDUCATION.0.topics.5.title: Fasting
EDUCATION.0.topics.5.content: The obligation of fasting Ramadan, what does and does not break the fast, fidyah and kaffarah.
EDUCATION.0.topics.6.title: Zakat
EDUCATION.0.topics.6.content: The nisab amount, who may receive zakat and how zakat is calculated.
EDUCATION.0.topics.7.title: Hajj
EDUCATION.0.topics.7.content: The obligatory parts of Hajj: ihram, standing at Arafat and the tawaf al-ziyarah. The wajib and sunnah acts of Hajj.
EDUCATION.1.title: Tajweed Rules
EDUCATION.1.description: Rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly
EDUCATION.1.topics.0.title: What is tajweed?
EDUCATION.1.topics.0.content: The science of reciting the Qur'an properly, giving each letter its correct point of articulation and qualities.
EDUCATION.1.topics.1.title: Points of articulation (makharij)
EDUCATION.1.topics.1.content: Where the letters come from: the throat, the tongue, the lips, the nasal passage and the mouth cavity.
EDUCATION.1.topics.2.title: Idgham
EDUCATION.1.topics.2.content: Merging one letter into the next. Idgham without ghunnah and idgham with ghunnah.
EDUCATION.1.topics.3.title: Ikhfa
EDUCATION.1.topics.3.content: Reciting a letter between clear pronunciation and merging, with ghunnah (nasalisation).
EDUCATION.1.topics.4.title: Izhar
EDUCATION.1.topics.4.content: Pronouncing a letter clearly without any change.
EDUCATION.1.topics.5.title: Iqlab
EDUCATION.1.topics.5.content: When ba comes after a nun sakinah, the nun is turned into a mim and recited with ghunnah.
EDUCATION.1.topics.6.title: Madd
EDUCATION.1.topics.6.content: Lengthening letters. Natural madd, connected madd and separated madd.
EDUCATION.1.topics.7.title: Stopping and starting (waqf and ibtida)
EDUCATION.1.topics.7.content: Stopping in the right places and starting again from the right places.

FAQ.0.questions.0.q: What is needed to become Muslim?
FAQ.0.questions.0.a: Saying the shahada is enough: "Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh" (I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger).
FAQ.0.questions.1.q: How many daily prayers are there?
FAQ.0.questions.1.a: Five daily prayers are obligatory: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha.
FAQ.0.questions.2.q: How many surahs does the Qur'an have?
FAQ.0.questions.2.a: The Qur'an consists of 114 surahs. The first is al-Fatiha and the last is an-Nas.
FAQ.0.questions.3.q: What is the nisab for zakat?
FAQ.0.questions.3.a: The nisab for zakat is the value of 80.18 grams of gold or 561.2 grams of silver. Muslims who own this amount for one full year are obliged to pay zakat.
FAQ.0.questions.4.a: Hajj is performed from the 8th to the 12th of Dhul-Hijjah. The standing at Arafat takes place on the Day of Arafah (9 Dhul-Hijjah).
FAQ.1.questions.0.a: Make the intention, wash the hands up to the wrists, rinse the mouth and nose, wash the face, wash the arms including the elbows, wipe the head, wipe the ears and wash the feet including the ankles.
FAQ.1.questions.1.a: Speaking, laughing, eating or drinking, losing ablution, turning away from the qibla and excessive movement invalidate the prayer.
FAQ.1.questions.2.q: When is the prostration of forgetfulness performed?
FAQ.1.questions.2.a: It is performed when a wajib act of the prayer is omitted or delayed, or when a fard act is delayed.
FAQ.1.questions.3.q: Is women's prayer different from men's?
FAQ.1.questions.3.a: It is essentially the same, with some differences in form (Hanafi): women raise their hands to shoulder level and keep their arms close to the ground in prostration.
FAQ.1.questions.4.q: What is the virtue of praying in congregation?
FAQ.1.questions.4.a: Prayer in congregation is 27 degrees more virtuous than praying alone (hadith).
FAQ.2.questions.0.a: Deliberately eating, drinking or having marital relations, inducing vomiting, nutritional injections and smoking break the fast.
FAQ.2.questions.1.q: What does not break the fast?
FAQ.2.questions.1.a: Eating or drinking by forgetfulness, giving blood, using eye drops and brushing the teeth (without swallowing) do not break the fast.
FAQ.2.questions.2.q: How much is the fidyah for fasting?
FAQ.2.questions.2.a: The fidyah is the amount needed to feed one poor person for one day. It is calculated according to the current guidance of your local religious authority.
FAQ.2.questions.3.a: In cases such as illness, pregnancy, breastfeeding, travel or old age one may not fast; the days are made up later or a fidyah is given.
